blocks.x: First, the hell he um... I mean, give him my uh, you don't want Jim Little do you?
We want to know all the ones that we have.
You want Sidney Brown?
No, is there any middle name?
No, no middle name.
And also Ralph Collins is there, and this is Bill Russell, and we're out at what is this, 1833 St. Anne.
Yeah.
On May the 27th about, is it? Yes, I guess. Pretty close, yeah, that's right. May the 27th. May the 27th, 1960. Mm-hmm. So, could you tell us just where you were born?
Oh, I born in a little country place by the name of Deerange. That was down on the other side of the river? Yeah. That's where Jim Robinson... That's where Jim Robinson from.
That was near Magnolia Plantation, was it? Well, it's a few miles from Magnolia. Uh, you know, there's a lot of musicians came from there, like Sonny Henry and the others that we know of.
Well, all the fellas just about from down that way, further down and coming up about three, four miles apart, you know?
And was Magnolia farther down the river? Yeah. It was farther down.
That's right.

How near were you to the river? Right on the river. Right on the river. Mm-hmm. Do you remember anything about the music when you were a kid down there? Did you hear any bands or anybody like guitar players, any music at all?

Well, I see, uh, when they had the music around there, well, they'd have a band room, you know? Yeah. And we'd go, we'd kids go around there and sit around, around the hall while they'd be taking music lessons.
Was that a band right in Deer Range?
Right in Deer Range.
They had a band right there.
Yeah, brass band. And, uh, they used to march around there on a Sunday. Yeah. One day a week. That's when my uncle was playing. And I come up after them.
What does his name, Brown do?
No. His name was, uh, D.D. Taylor.
What did he play?
He played drum, bass drum. Bass drum. Mm-hmm. Um, great.
I was, I was looking at this, uh, I was wondering if that wind is blowing without a fan turned on there.
Yeah, it's a fan in the back. Oh, you can pull that wind down.

Oh, no, I'm sorry. No, it's alright. Let me see. No, it's alright. It seemed to be, uh, picking up something. I guess it's just the wind blowing through there. Yeah. No, leave the fan on. It's nice and cool. I was wondering what that was. I couldn't figure out. Okay, excuse me for interrupting. Uh, did anybody else in your family play? Your father or anybody play? Well, no.
My, my daddy, I never know my daddy. Oh. I never know. He, he, uh, he died just about in the time I'm born. Mm-hmm.
How big a town was that?
Oh, it was a little small place. This was a plantation.

Oh, it was a plantation too then. I didn't know for sure. Well, Jim didn't tell you that? No, he never did tell me. He never said much about, you know, what kind of a town it was. Mm-hmm. We talked to Sonny Henry and we knew Magnolia was a plantation. Yeah, well. He never told us that's what Deer Range was.
Deer Range was a plantation like Magnolia. All right.
Um, I was asking about the plantation there. Jim told us it's all under water now, I think. Well.

He said it's all gone. It's just a little island. It's like an island now. It's, let's see, about there. The river might come about from here to Cleveland Street. That's a good block, you know. Yeah. And from the railroad track going up and down, it's water all that side. From the railroad track back to the lake.
Did that railroad always run down there when you were a boy? Oh, yeah.
That was a railroad from long years back. That was the first road. Well, they didn't have any other railroad down there. Is that on the road to Bureus?
Yeah.

That's the Bureus Road. On down the road? That'll go all the way down to Fort St. Philip. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Was it a big place, isn't it? Oh, it's a big place going straight up and down, you know. Oh, I see. Yeah, a lot. Yeah, it's long, but it's not wide. Uh-huh. What did they grow there, mainly? What did they grow there, mainly? Coming to New Orleans, you see. Coming to Algiers. Coming to Algiers. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. Now, it's a big place going straight up and down, you know. Oh, I see. Yeah, a lot. Yeah, it's long, but it's not wide. Uh-huh.
What did they grow there, mainly?

They used to grow sugarcane from magnolia up this way. Coming to New Orleans, you see. Coming to Algiers. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. All sugarcane. Now, there's no more sugarcane down there. It's just truck forms. Oh, truck forms.
Yeah.
Uh-huh. Like you and I would have a piece of land we were cultivated in trucking, you see.
And when you were a boy, did you do any work on the farm there?
Uh, well, I was, uh, I would work by a grocery store.
Oh, you know, I forgot to ask just when you were born, too. We didn't ask that to get your birthday.
Yeah.
You want that right now? Yeah, you might as well put it in that, how we think of it.
Yeah. I was born in July. July the 19th, 1894.
Well, just how are you related to Jim Robinson? We might as well get that family.

Oh, yeah, well, Jim is my uncle. He's my mother's brother. And, uh, well, we would live just about, he would be his, with his sister down that way, his mother was dead, see. And up this way further would be my house.
About how many houses were there?
Oh, there was quite a few houses. Yeah, they had, they had a little town, just about a mile from there. Oh, that's still the Deer Ridge, you know.
Oh, I see.
And, uh, the next place down further is Junior. The next place is Woodland.
And you say you worked in the grocery store there? Yeah. How many grocery stores would that be?
One. Just the one? One grocery store.
What would you use this be, that a clerk or a?

Well, yes, work around, in stores. Well, when he'd go to lunch, you know, I'd hand the grocery all by myself, you see. And, well, I was a water boy at the time. And they took me off of water boy and they brought me to store. Well, stay there a while.
Did you ever think of, uh, try to play a musical instrument at that time? Yes, I learned violin at the time.
Oh, I see. In the store, why didn't you go to the store? Yeah. Where did you get your first instrument, remember? Where did you get your violin or? Yeah, well down there at that place, Deer Ridge.
And I, when I went down further to Beers, well I went across the river, it's the oyster factory
over there, you know, and we played, what was it said then Sunday nights for Adam Nunez.
Did you have any lessons on violin or pick it up?
No, I know, I didn't, I didn't put lessons on that. Um, I just learned that by hitting. Yeah. The mandolin, that, and the guitar.
Can you tell us any more about that brass band, who was the leader or how it was organized?

Well, that would be hard for me to call men's name now, just quite a few years back, you know. Sure. Well, I would say my uncle, he was the drummer. And my step daddy was the trumpet player. And I know Alec Taylor, Ben Cole, Ben Kelly, Chris Kelly, Walter Johnson, that was a good bass player like me. He used to play the big hornets. Big girl. Big girl. And Alec Taylor, Ben Kelly, oh I call Ben Kelly's name huh? Yeah.
I think with Chris Kelly in those days, was he older than you?
Yeah, well not much different. Not much different between him and I. Might be three or four years or something like that.
Was Ben Kelly any relation to Chris?
Yeah, that's two brothers.
Oh, they were brothers. What did Ben play?

I think Ben used to play alto. And Chris was on the cornet? Yeah. About how big a band was it? Oh, it was ten to twelve men's, you know. And you said they played on Sunday, was there any place to parade around there much? Well they would just walk around, up and down the road, you know. And when the train would pass during the Sunday evening, well they would go and meet the train, you see? Oh yeah. And the train would pass there and the people that was on there would enjoy listening to them playing, you see? Oh yeah, I see. Yeah. Oh man, about ten to fifteen minutes. Oh that's all? That's all. Then they'd go to the band room and rehearsal again, you see?
Oh yeah, I see. Yeah. Did you ever have any funerals down there that the band would play for?
No, that would be very certain. They would have somebody die around there. Yeah, wouldn't be very many people in there.
Not many people.

Were there very Well you know that would be a hurry up funeral see. They didn't even bond people that they did you see. They would maybe have to die early that morning. They'd get rid of them that evening. Sometimes it might keep them until the next day. So that place just washed away down there. They had perverse. They let it bust and everything washed away. So we left there. Was that the reason you came to do All In? Well no I left ahead of that but I used to go down there once in a while you know.
About when did you move up here? When did I move around here?

Oh yeah. Oh just about 19, between 1912 and 13. And what I wouldn't forget about going down there. I'd go down there once in a while. Maybe sometime we'd go from here down to the end of the road. Verus, Ostricker, Sikola Canal and.
I forgot what Jim Robinson told us. Had he moved up here already at that time? Do you remember?
Oh around that time. Around. Yeah Jim and I came here just about the same time.
Was he playing any instrument in those days? Oh he was playing the ghetto a bit.
I knew he started on guitar. He was playing guitar. Yeah. I think Jim learned the trombone in the army.
I think it's the absence of you told me. Yeah. When you came to New Orleans in New York, were you looking for a music job or why did you come to New Orleans?

No I come here to live then. And we got together Sam Morgan and I got together right at that time you see. And we had a little six piece band around then. What were you playing then? I was playing violin. Violin. Uh huh. And it's a little while after I, I wasn't finished growing at the time. And just about the time I was getting big enough to, that I could get tall enough to reach a bass you know? And then I got my Uncle B's violin. Because he had quit playing that time.
stuff
No, he was another one. I had several uncles around me. And I got...
What was his name by the way, do you remember?

F.B. Robinson. Jim's brother. And I flew around a little while and I think you learned how to play pretty good you see. And I knew Sonny Henry, was a nice musician, and I went with him and I took, he started me out on the bass, on the bass horn and the fiddle, see. Then I went with Sam Morgan for True at that time, see. All the way. I was a Sam Morgan man from that time and Sam Morgan got, he did get crippled.
Sam Morgan was a little older than you I guess wasn't he?
Well, it might have been a few years different, but not much.
Did he already have a band when you first met him? Yeah. You already had some?
Yeah. Well I was playing, I played with Sam a while and his brother Isaiah, I played with him a while. Well I played with the Morgan boys the most. And...
Were they together in the same band then or each had...

No, they had two different bands at the time. They had Young Morgan and they had original Sam Morgan at the time. Well I played with both of them. When I didn't have anything to do I'd work with Sam, you see. Well at that time there wasn't many musicians. Couldn't go around and play, you know. Well a band would get together and at that time they would stick together, you see.
By the way, where did you live when you moved up here? I uh...
What part of town?
In this Tremé.
Right around the Tremé. I never lived anywhere else.
So Sam Morgan right in that section? All in that section.
That's what I thought. I wanted to ask you, Sidney, had Chris Kelly left the Deerange before you left or do you remember just when he left?
No, I guess we all left there just about the same time because after the crevasse the levee bust loose.
How long after you left did the levee break?
Oh right around that town.
Oh, very shortly after.

Yeah. And it didn't do any good to go around there because there wasn't nothing to do. No. All the plantation was under water. When the water did go into the, from the levee to the woods, well it just stayed there. And it got to be a real fish pond. Oh yeah. Yeah.
Well I guess all the members of that brass band that they had there, I guess they all came to New Orleans. Well they did.
They left and they went different places you see. They didn't all come here. They went maybe to the other side of the river. They were very beautiful.
And um. But both of the Kellys came to New Orleans?
Yeah, both of them. Well Chris Kelley's brother, Ben Kelley, he's living yet. Oh is that so?
Mm-hmm. Is he around in this neighborhood, you know where he is?
I uh, he lived over in that project over there, but I wouldn't know where.
Over the La Pate project?
Yes. I wouldn't know exactly where he lived.
We'll find him sometimes.
I see him once in a while.
Would you want to find him? Yeah, we'd like to talk to him too.
It would be wonderful.
Yeah. That would be a good idea, wouldn't it? Yeah.

So many people know about Chris, but he's not here to tell us anything himself. Yeah. And his brother could tell us about Chris too. That is right. Is Chris more famous than, did Ben ever do much in music up here?

Oh, Ben never did do much playing like Chris did. I didn't think so. No. After the brass band quit playing, well that was the end of Ben, you see? Yeah. There wasn't no more Ben, but Chris Kelly, he came here and he got organized and he got in a band playing around too.
Did you ever play with him up here?
Oh, I played several jobs with him.
What kind of a band did he have then? Oh, no, not much of a band. I mean did they play arrangements and read music or just head? Oh yeah, they would read. They would read.
They were all readers. They were all readers. Yeah, what I say, not good readers either. They would spill, you know? Spill.
Do you remember who else was in the band about the time you played with him? Oh, no.
Them, that fellow, they're dead now. Chris Kelly, he's dead and the one who was playing with him is dead.
They're all gone.
Yeah, Chris Kelly, I know a couple of fellows used to play with him. One fellow by the name of Duck Onus.
You heard of him? Duck.
Yeah, well he was playing with Triss and Jim Ebron.
Was that a bass player?
No, he was clarinet man.
Clarinet, oh yeah.
So that's about all I can see on Chris Kelly and Sam Morgan.
Do you remember some people said he was very good on the blues. Do you remember how he played? Oh yeah, he was top of the blues.
Really good. Oh yeah, he was good. And his real blues was Kelly's Love. Yeah. And boy, he was the best band around here on that.
So, did the Eddle play any, do you ever remember him playing any blues out of the D-Range?
No, no. I, no. I never know him to play any blues out of the D-Range.
You just played the brass band? Yes. Good.

I was going to ask some more about your days, early days before the war with Sam Morgan. Where you played, what kind of jobs you had in the beginning. Do you remember your very first job that you got paid for? Oh, around the city here?
Yeah. Well, oh yeah, we used to play at the Colony Hall. Where at? At the, the Hope's Hall. And at the Santa Teresa. Where was that?
I don't know that one.

That was up, up in the Gordon District. Or uptown. Mm-hmm. We used to play up, up there on a Saturday night, and play at Estore. Yeah, the hotel over on the drive-the-Range. Yeah. Played there on a Sunday night. Well, we had Saturday night, Sunday night, Monday night. That's about three to a week.
Where did you play Monday night?
Oh, we didn't do anything Monday night.
Oh, Monday, I thought. No. Somebody told me they used to have dances at the Economy Hall some night. Oh, yes, that's true.

At the Economy, was every Monday night. That was on Monday. Mm-hmm. That was, that would be Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. You mentioned Monday, then. You had to go to Monday. Yeah. And, at the Saint Sue Hall. That was up on Howard.
Oh, yeah. It's still there. Yeah. Yeah. Um, yeah.

I believe they have, uh, what's this boy's name? Around that, uh, place up there. It's a big nightclub he's got up there. Yeah. What is it there? That's near the Dutron. That's, that's the place. But I don't think it's the same building. No, it's just right in, it's in the same block. Yeah.
Is that the pool hall, did you say you were in that route one time? Uh, the old Saint Sue.
Yeah. Yeah, I think they have a pool hall in there now. Yeah, I think that's all connection to the one.
I don't know, I didn't notice that. You had to go through a courtyard and the dance hall was in back. Yeah. And the little sittin' back. That's right.
That's right. And the dance hall was in the back. Uh-huh. I went in there and it's just a pool hall now. Yeah.
You just have pool tables in there. I wouldn't know how it's located, you know. Mm-hmm.

Yeah. I don't know. I didn't notice that, you had to go through a courtyard and the dance hall was in back. Yeah. And the little sittin' back. That's right. That's right. And the dance hall was in the back. Uh-huh. I went in there and it's just a pool hall now. Yeah. You just have pool tables in there. I haven't been around that place in so long.
I wouldn't know how it's located, you know. It looked like a nice hall though, a nice big hall. Yeah. I thought one time the dude dropped was, I thought they was connected together.
The dude drops right on the street there, I think, on Howard.
Yes, it's on the front.
Right on the front. Mm-hmm. But it's up in the next building or something. Yeah. A little bit farther up top.
Mm-hmm.
Anyway, I was going to ask some more about the Sam Morgan Band. Who else was in it, if you remember the other men at that time?

Yeah, well, Sam Morgan Band, it was Sam playing trumpet, Yank playing trombone, and his brother used to play trombone too. Buddy. Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson. And Galle was the banjo. And Sam Morgan trumpet. Did they have a bass player then, before you? Yes, they had a bass player before me at that time. And I'll finish telling you about the other man or two, what Sam Morgan had. For Alfred Williams. Mm-hmm. He had Alfred playing drums.
And Joe Watson playing clarinet. You heard about Joe Watson playing clarinet. Did they have a bass player then?
Before you? Yes, they had a bass player before me at that time. And I'll finish telling you about the other man or two, what Sam Morgan had. But Sam Morgan had he had Alfred playing drums.
For Alfred Williams.
And Joe Watson playing clarinet. You heard about Joe Watson?
Yeah I heard of him.
And a little while after that Sam got crippled. Well he didn't work then for a while then that band broke up.
That was way back. That wasn't the late years when he had a stroke. You don't mean that or anything.
That's the time he had a stroke.
Oh he had a stroke. That's what I wondered.
Yeah that's the time.

Was Isaiah Morgan, I forget that he told me, was he older than Sam? No he was a young man. He was a younger. That's why they called it the young Morgan. I was thinking he was older than Sam maybe. That's not right.
Well after that Sam got well enough to go about and play it and he put the band as one band you see. Young Morgan went in with Sam Morgan and they made one band. Well that was still named Sam Morgan.
And Jim Robinson came in much later than you didn't he?
Yeah later than I.

I was wondering about that very first band before the first world war you played with them too you said. Yes. Well who was the drummer then do you remember right back? Well yeah Sam drummer. Sam drummer before the war. Yeah. And uh Yang and all of them played with him then back before the war.
Yeah at that time.
Jim Robinson of course wasn't playing with the war.

Well now Jim didn't learn, didn't know anything about Tram Horn at the time. Jim well Jim went in the war and he stayed about a year and a half or two years and came back where he was then he started out of playing.
Well can you tell us about when you went in the Army and your experiences as you playing any band in the Army?

Well when I went in, I didn't fool around playing over on this side at all and when we went to the other side, I started playing. I got, we met a band in the orchestra right in the Army and they made us go with the entertaining department. Well then we stayed in Paris, France a good while. We used to go, they had seven hospitals. We used to go from one to the other see. And we stayed around there about six or eight months. And then I, then I got sick. And I go, I went to the hospital. And I stayed there about seven or eight months. And it was a long time before I got back to my outfit. And now...
I didn't catch you with my outfit until we come here, back to the States.
When did you take up the bass or the tuba and all? Was that in the Army or after the war?
No, that was after that.
After the war?
Yeah, we had a little entertaining outfit over there, you see.
You just played violin all the time?
Yeah, with the YMCA around there.
Any other fellows from New Orleans in the group?
No, the fellows from New York.
How did their music compare the music you had down here? Was it anything like it? Did it swing like it did down here?

Well, I don't think it was much different because they were just learning to it, you see. Yeah. They were just learning any, well we didn't know much about it. Other than that we didn't know much about it. Just what we got out of it, it was all right, you see. Yeah. And, well I did full run in France. I wasn't doing nothing. I was no good, no service in the outfit when I was there. I was sick for a while. I spent two years in the old man. I was doing nothing with this side and that side, you see. Because I was in a hospital pretty good while. I never counted the months I was sick.
Okay, it's going again. I was going to ask a little bit more about that band that you played with in the Army. What kind of music they used? Were they just late, popular pieces or old songs?
Well, we had just enough ground that they entertained the soldiers and the nurses in the hospital, you see. And we'd go out every night.

Did they play any pieces like the jazz numbers they do now? Played it on the Archer Blues or Tiger Rag or any of the old New Orleans numbers. You know like they play down here. Still getting a little wind blowing there.
No, well I had to play what they had in their view, you know? Yeah.
We'd play blues over there and get some of that breeze.
Well we'd get round there and rehearse. The numbers were dead though, you see?
Yeah. They didn't play any blues that much.
No, no, no blues. No blues whatever.
Or any of the old Dixieland numbers and things of that kind.

No. No. And well it wasn't much jazz around that time, no. Yeah. Because I was with the boys from New York and they'd know something and I'd know something, you see. So. You played lead on your violin.
Yeah. What other instruments did you do?
Listen we had a guitar, a violin, a trap drum, and a trumpet. That's all. That's all we had, Ronnie. Just four. And.
You never played in any brass band then before that time or up to that time?
No. The time I played in brass band after I came back and after I learned that, you know?
How did you take up the tuba then? How did you take up that big instrument?

Well I was with Sam Morgan at the time. Oh you were playing with him again then? Yeah. Yeah. I was playing with Sam Morgan at the time and they quit using the baseball you see. And I just picked that thing up and I said well I'll be if I can learn it. Three or four weeks I had that and gone. And me and Sam Morgan, brother Albert, Albert Morgan. Yeah. I know him. Yeah. We started learning the horn again. But he was playing with Faith Morgan on the boat. See? Yeah. And uh, Sonny Henry took me on that and uh, Fiddler learned, learned music then. I had to learn music to play that you see. Yeah. But playing the biggest I was playing with my head. What kind of a horn did you have when you first, did you have one of these

wrap around here or just an upright tuba? No. Upright tuba. Is it B flat or E flat? E flat tuba. E flat. Well that's, that's an E flat tuba. Oh is that E flat? Yeah that's an E flat up there. I thought most of the big things, Pelican and Suzy Phones were B flat. But that's an E flat. Yeah. That's all you ever played in the E flat tuba. I didn't know.

Nah, I used to hit it too. Yeah, sounds good. You know I used to play for you. Yeah, you hit a couple of records for me. Yeah. I played the bass tuba with you and uh, and slow drag played the bass tuba. Yeah, that's one of them started with Buck. That's right. And that's from Johnson time.
1944 over at San Jacinto Hall. Yeah, that's right. That was a pretty good time wasn't it Bill? Yeah.

And uh, then I started out with this making street parades and I had more work than I could handle. Which bands did you play with? I played with all of the bands around here. That's uh, I played with the Tuxedo. That's John Kazmi. And uh, George William. He had a good brass band at the time. Oh man, there's so many old brass bands at the time. Some bands didn't have no name.

That's right, I remember some of the bands. That's right, I remember some of the bands that get up the group. Yeah. I remember some times you'd be with the people like uh, Kid Howard, Matthew Williams, and they organized bands. Yeah, that's right. And they organized bands. Yeah. And George Lewis.

Just get up a band. Just say, well we'll get up a bunch of fellas and make bands. See, no name. Yeah. Well, that was it. And it went a little further. And the road got so bad of playing on the road. Going out. Making night here and night there and the night next place. That was with Sam Morgan band, you name it? Yeah. Well, we used to go, when I was with Sam Morgan band, we used to go Pensacola, Mobile, Bloxy, Gulfport, and Hattiesbury. Then we'd come on back in town, you see? Mm-hmm. And we'd have a Saturday night play and Sunday night play and a Monday night play. Then we'd go on the road around like Tuesday. Tuesday. Tuesday. Oh, maybe. Yeah. Yeah. Well, it went around like that for a while and I got tired playing. I got tired of the road and I went back to work in the packing house for lodging on Collins. By what year would that be? That would be in 28.
What did you pack? What kind of a place? Packing house. Oh, meat? Yeah, meat house.

Which one was it? Hmm? Which one? Longinor and Collins. That's a local house, you know. Oh, I see. Did you still land? Oh, they did. The old man died. Longinor died and then old man Collins died right maybe a year or so behind, you see. And then I got in bad luck. I had to quit working in the packing house because I got crippled. About how long were you there? How long I worked there? Oh, about 20 years. In the packing house. That's all. I made records with you and I was working there. Working there. I didn't know where you were working. At the same time. I didn't know. See. And well, when I was making records with you, I'd be maybe get off that night that I'd make records for you early for the night and then maybe go back there around 12, 1 o'clock. See?
Well, you were still playing music right now while you worked there. While I was working for Bill. But otherwise, I mean, you were playing, you even played parades in those days too.

Oh, yeah. Well, that would be Sunday. Yeah. I mean, Sunday, that's the only time that they have parades, unless they have a day of funeral, you see. That was going to be a couple hours. You never put the music down? No, not completely, no. No. It went on like that and depression come on. It didn't pay the fool around with music. There was nothing to it. So, I almost put the bass in the corner and didn't play nothing. I'd get a job with a fellow to come at me and play on a Saturday night or a Sunday night. I'd be so tired. I wouldn't. I'd turn them down. I'd turn them down. And, uh, went on like that and then after I finished telling you about at the packing house, I had to quit there because I was crippled in there, you see? Mm-hmm. And, uh, that happened in 45. I had to give up. And I stayed 45, 46, 47, and then I passed an operation. And after I passed that operation, then Papa Celeste had come by and seen me. I was doing pretty good, you know? Yeah. And, uh, he said, Jim, you playing any music yet? I said, no, I'm not playing now, Papa. I'm just about to give up. I believe. I believe I want you to play with my band. I said, all right. And I just got my stuff together and went and joined with him. And after I played with him a while and I began to like it. And then, went along pretty good. And he was the one I finished up with. Yeah, I played with Papa from, uh, from, uh, 48 up until 59.
That's when Eddie Pearson had the band in the last couple years.
Yes. Eddie died two years. Eddie had been dead two years now, ain't he?
Not quite. A little over a year, I guess. Over a year, yeah.

It was, uh, around Christmas time passed, that was one year. Yeah, it's about three and six months. Yeah. And after Eddie died one, I didn't stay there long. No, that's right. I came in last year in July. And I had arthritis so bad I had to pull myself off the road. We come from, uh, Florida. And I was on the fifth of July. And I didn't, I didn't go back anymore. So, I finished up last year.
Were most of your dates with Salaside on the road or parties around here? Where did you work with Salaside?
Well, with Papa Band, we had plenty of work. Somehow we couldn't do it all. We had work in the city.
